summary: Describes version 1 of the Sender Policy Framework, which lets a domain say which hosts may send email using its name. It targets forged return paths and forged HELO names. It is an experimental document and was replaced by RFC 7208.

eli5.summary: A domain can publish a list of mail servers allowed to send for it. Receivers check the list so fake mail is easier to spot.

subtitle: How a domain publishes, in DNS, which mail servers may send email using its name, and how receivers check it.

tldr.problem: Email protocols let any sending host claim any domain in the SMTP HELO/EHLO command or the MAIL FROM reverse-path, which makes forged senders easy and spam hard to reduce.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes an SPF record in DNS listing which hosts may use its name, and a receiver runs the check_host() function on the connecting IP address and the claimed identity to get a result such as Pass or Fail.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4408 is an Experimental document that was replaced by RFC 7208 and later updated by RFC 6652.

today: RFC 4408 is an Experimental document that has been obsoleted by RFC 7208, and it was updated by RFC 6652. Use RFC 7208 for the current SPF specification.

sections.title: The Forged Sender Problem
sections.content:
In today's email system, any host injecting mail can identify itself as any domain name it likes, at the session, envelope or header level. The RFC calls this a major obstacle to reducing unsolicited bulk email, and notes that many domain holders worry about others using their names with malicious intent.

The Sender Policy Framework (SPF) lets a domain owner authorize the hosts that may use its domain in the MAIL FROM or HELO identity. Receivers test the sending Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) against the published record. After a successful check, policy can be based on the domain's reputation rather than on a host IP address, and a failed check allows stronger action such as rejection.

An IESG note says this document was published as Experimental with no general technical consensus, alongside the Sender ID documents (RFC 4405, RFC 4406 and RFC 4407), and warns of serious open issues and of conflicts when the two approaches share DNS records.
sections.eli5: Right now anyone can write any return address on an envelope. SPF lets the real owner of an address say which post offices are allowed to send mail with it.

sections.title: Identities and Results
sections.content:
SPF checks two identities. The HELO identity comes from the SMTP HELO or EHLO command. The MAIL FROM identity comes from the SMTP MAIL command; if the reverse-path is null, it is defined as the localpart postmaster at the HELO domain. Clients MUST check MAIL FROM, and it is RECOMMENDED that they also check HELO separately. Checking other identities without the domain owner's approval is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The check should happen during the SMTP transaction, so errors can be returned in SMTP replies. The outcome is one of seven results:

  • None: no record was published, or no checkable domain was found.
  • Neutral: the owner makes no statement; it must be treated exactly like None.
  • Pass: the client is authorized.
  • Fail: the client is explicitly not authorized. A receiver that rejects SHOULD use SMTP reply code 550 and the 5.7.1 DSN code.
  • SoftFail: between Fail and Neutral; receivers SHOULD NOT reject on this alone.
  • TempError: a transient error; a rejection SHOULD use reply code 451 and DSN code 4.4.3.
  • PermError: the published records could not be correctly interpreted.
sections.eli5: The guard can say "yes, on the list", "definitely not on the list", "not sure", or "my list is broken". Each answer tells the mail room what to do next.

sections.title: The SPF Record
sections.content:
An SPF record is a DNS resource record that says which hosts are and are not authorized to use a domain name. It is one string of text, for example v=spf1 +mx a:colo.example.com/28 -all. It starts with the version v=spf1, followed by directives. Each directive is an optional qualifier plus a mechanism.

The qualifiers map to results: a plus sign gives Pass and is the default, a minus sign (as in -all) gives Fail, a tilde (as in ~all) gives SoftFail and a question mark (as in ?all) gives Neutral. Records are published at the host name they apply to, as either a TXT record or the new SPF record type, code 99, with identical content. The RFC says a compliant domain SHOULD publish both types and MUST publish at least one. A domain MUST NOT have multiple records that would both be selected.

Multiple strings in one DNS record are concatenated without spaces. To avoid falling back to TCP, answers should fit within 512 octets, which is likely if the DNS name and record text total under 450 characters. It is RECOMMENDED that records end in -all or redirect to one that does.
sections.eli5: The list is a single line of text stored in the domain's public address book. Each item on the line says "this group may send" or "this group may not".

sections.title: Evaluating a Record with check_host()
sections.content:
The check_host() function takes the client IP address <ip>, the <domain> to look up and the <sender> identity. If the domain is malformed or does not exist (RCODE 3), it returns None immediately. If every DNS lookup fails or times out, it returns TempError.

The function keeps only records that begin exactly with v=spf1, and discards TXT records if any SPF-type record exists. Two or more remaining records give PermError; none gives None. Mechanisms are then tried from left to right, and the first match returns its qualifier's result. If nothing matches and there is no redirect modifier, the result is Neutral.

The mechanisms are:

  • all: always matches; used last as a default.
  • include: recursively evaluates another domain; only a Pass there counts as a match.
  • a and mx: match the addresses of a host or of a domain's mail exchangers; at most 10 MX names may be looked up.
  • ptr: reverse-DNS check, discouraged because it is slow and burdens the arpa name servers.
  • ip4 and ip6: match an address or a CIDR network.
  • exists: matches if an A record exists for a constructed name.

Two modifiers exist. redirect= hands evaluation to another domain's record when nothing matches. exp= names a TXT record that supplies an explanation string for a Fail result. The RFC admits that the name include was poorly chosen in hindsight, since only the evaluated result of the other record is used.
sections.eli5: The guard reads the list from left to right. The first line that fits the arriving bus decides the answer. If no line fits, the answer is "not sure".

sections.title: Macros and the Received-SPF Header
sections.content:
Domain-spec arguments and explanation strings can use macros written %{letter}. Letters include s (sender), l (local part), o (sender domain), d (domain), i (client IP), p (validated domain name of the IP), v (in-addr or ip6) and h (HELO domain). Transformers can keep the right-hand parts or reverse them: with client IP 192.0.2.1, %{ir} expands to 1.2.0.192. This allows DNSBL-style lookups such as exists:%{ir}.sbl.spamhaus.example.org.

Receivers are RECOMMENDED to record the result in a Received-SPF trace header field, prepended above the receiver's own Received field. It carries the result, an optional comment and key-value pairs such as client-ip, envelope-from, helo, identity, mechanism, problem and receiver.
sections.eli5: Macros are fill-in-the-blank slots in the list, such as "put the visitor's address here". The receiving office also stamps the answer on the letter so the recipient can see it.

sections.title: Implications and Security
sections.content:
SPF breaks some legitimate mail flows. Mailing lists usually rewrite MAIL FROM, so they fit. Forwarding services and aliases are harder, because forwarded mail arrives from a host the original domain never listed. The RFC suggests remedies such as rewriting the envelope sender, trusting known forwarders, or whitelisting them. The authorization check also generally precludes arbitrary MTA relays between sender and receiver, so published records must cover the border MTAs that actually send across the Internet.

The processing limits are strict, to stop denial-of-service amplification. Implementations MUST limit mechanisms and modifiers that cause DNS lookups to at most 10 per check, counting include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect. Exceeding this gives PermError. A time limit, if imposed, SHOULD allow at least 20 seconds and then return TempError.

Other cautions: an SPF pass does not make other identities such as the From header trustworthy; DNS data and the client IP address could be spoofed; SPF cannot stop one user of an MTA forging another user of the same MTA; and explanation strings come from the sender's domain and may be malicious or misleading. DNS queries can also reveal who is sending mail and where it is going.
sections.eli5: The guard's list only tells which buses are allowed, not whether the passenger is honest. And the guard must not spend all day looking things up, so there is a limit of ten lookups per check.

items.label: Pass
items.desc: The client is authorized to send with this identity.

items.label: Fail
items.desc: The client is explicitly not authorized; may be rejected with reply code 550.

items.label: SoftFail
items.desc: Probably not authorized, but the domain will not say so strongly; do not reject on this alone.

items.label: Neutral
items.desc: The owner makes no assertion; treated exactly like None.

items.label: None
items.desc: No record or no checkable domain.

items.label: TempError
items.desc: Transient error such as a DNS timeout; reply code 451 if rejecting.

items.label: PermError
items.desc: The published record could not be correctly interpreted.
